name: Jackson Pr. 12.5: E×B runaway
description: Jackson Problem 12.5 and §12.3. Crossed fields make a particle drift only if $|E| < c|B|$: then a frame moving with $\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{B}/B^2$ sees no electric field. Here the electric field is stronger than c times the magnetic one (c = 2 cells per time unit), no such frame exists, and the particle runs away along E. Near a magnet the field is strong enough: place magnets so that the particle drifts into the detector instead.

reality.represents: Crossed fields with |E| > c|B|: no frame to drift in (Jackson Pr. 12.5)

remarks.line: No frame without an electric field
remarks.detail: When |E| > c|B| no moving frame cancels E (E² − c²B² is the same in every frame), and the particle runs away along E, exactly as relativity says.

c is a few cells per time unit, so that the board spans less than a wavelength of the RF and the particle crosses it in a few periods; the physics depends only on such ratios (v/c, the wavelength against the board), which real devices share.
The particle's charge is small and every field large (only qE and qB matter), so that its radiation stays below the accuracy.

A uniformly magnetized sphere has exactly a dipole's field outside it, which keeps the field simple and exact; real magnets are blocks, rings and pole pieces, and an instrument's magnet makes a field as uniform as it can.
